source_refs.note: Topic 7.4, printed pages 173-174: sequence homology, orthologs and paralogs, and structural homology.

blocks.title: Sequence homology
blocks.text: Sequence homology is the similarity between DNA, RNA or protein sequences due to shared ancestry. Homologous sequences have evolved from a common ancestral sequence.

Homologous sequences fall into two main types. Orthologs are sequences in different species that originated from a common ancestral gene during speciation; orthologs often retain the same function across species. Paralogs are sequences within the same species that originated by gene duplication; paralogs can evolve new functions even though they arose from the same ancestral gene.

blocks.alt: A tree read from left to right. Ancestral Histone H1 gene splits at the Gene duplication line into Histone H1.1 (red) and Histone H1.2 (blue). At the Speciation line each copy goes to Human and to Chimpanzee, giving Human histone H1.1, Human histone H1.2, Chimpanzee histone H1.1 and Chimpanzee histone H1.2. A small bracket marks the two human genes as Paralog; a long bracket joins Human histone H1.1 and Chimpanzee histone H1.1 as Ortholog.

blocks.text: Sequence homology gives insight into the evolutionary relationships between organisms: by comparing homologous sequences, scientists can infer the evolutionary history and divergence of species. It also gives a clue to the function of an unknown gene or protein: if an unknown gene or protein is homologous to one with a known function, it is likely to have a similar function. And identifying homologous genes involved in diseases across different species helps in understanding disease mechanisms and developing treatments, since homologous genes in model organisms can be studied to gain insight into human diseases.

blocks.title: Structural homology
blocks.text: Structural homology is the similarity in the three-dimensional structures of proteins or other macromolecules due to shared ancestry. Proteins with similar structures often perform similar functions, even if their sequences are not highly similar.

The three-dimensional structure of a protein gives critical information about its function, so understanding structural homology helps in predicting the function of newly discovered proteins. It is crucial in drug design, because drugs are often designed to interact with specific protein structures, and understanding the structural relationships between proteins helps in designing more effective drugs. Studying the structural homology of proteins also helps in understanding the evolutionary processes that shape protein functions and interactions.
